title: How the symphony grew
subtitle: From Haydn’s sudden chord to Mahler’s last few strings

hero.caption: A concert in London’s Hanover Square Rooms. Engraving in The Illustrated London News, 24 June 1843.

intro: At the Hanover Square Rooms in 1792, Haydn startles London with a single chord. A little over a century later, the last page of Mahler’s Ninth needs only strings, soft enough to make the gaps between phrases feel enormous.

stations.title: Haydn sets a trap
stations.text: London, 23 March 1792. At Salomon’s concert in the Hanover Square Rooms, Haydn’s new symphony lets the strings play a tune of almost nursery simplicity. They repeat it more softly. Then the whole orchestra lands on one fortissimo chord, with timpani. The joke has survived two centuries of advance warning. Haydn wrote the symphony during his first London visit; the slow movement turns its little C-major tune into a set of variations. In the first, the second violins and violas keep the melody while the first violins run semiquavers around it.

cues.text: The strings begin a little C-major tune, with a bass note at the start of each bar.
The quiet repeat ends with a single fortissimo chord from the whole orchestra, including timpani.
The first violins run semiquavers around the tune, now held by second violins and violas.

stations.title: Mozart comes home by another road
stations.text: Three years before Haydn’s London visit, Mozart wrote his G-minor Symphony, K. 550. Its opening violin figure has a nervous insistence: in the development, scraps of it pass between strings and winds, each repetition landing somewhere less settled. Mozart then brings the opening back to G minor. The return is longer than the first statement because the bridge between the themes keeps travelling. And the second theme, which first appeared in B♭ major, comes back in G minor. Its gentle phrases sound pinched and darker now, with semitones rubbing together in the woodwind and strings.

cues.text: Scraps of the opening violin figure pass between instruments and through changing keys.
The opening returns in G minor; the bridge between the themes now takes a longer route.
The second theme comes back in G minor, darkening its earlier B♭-major phrases.

stations.title: Mozart fits five tunes together
stations.text: By the end of the Jupiter finale, the orchestra seems crowded with people who all have something to say. The four-note tune C–D–F–E keeps its long notes while quicker figures hurry past it; one part can begin before another has finished. Mozart wrote this symphony in the same summer of 1788 as the G-minor. Here the return to C major has still more work ahead. Five themes fit together in the coda, each keeping its own rhythm as they pass between the instruments. Trumpets and timpani join the final C-major chords.

cues.text: The four-note tune returns in C major, with quicker figures moving around it.
Five themes fit together in the coda: long notes cross paths with running figures and short replies.
Trumpets and timpani reinforce the final C-major chords as the running lines converge.

stations.title: Beethoven stops for an oboe
stations.text: The Fifth’s opening rhythm keeps working long after its first thunderous statement. In the development it passes between instruments and through changing keys; eventually the exchanges shrink to isolated chords, with silence between the replies. When the opening returns at bar 248, winds and brass reinforce it. Then Beethoven does something astonishingly small. At bar 268 the orchestra stops, leaving an oboe alone in an Adagio. A whole argument waits for one player to finish. Later, bassoons take the call previously played by horns, and the second theme returns in C major, a minor third below its earlier E♭ major.

cues.text: The opening rhythm travels through new pitches and keys as the development begins.
Winds and strings exchange slow chords; the replies grow shorter, with rests between them.
The opening returns, with winds and brass reinforcing its short-note rhythm.
At bar 268 the orchestra pauses and one oboe plays an unaccompanied Adagio.
Bassoons take the horns’ old call before the second theme returns in C major.

stations.title: Brahms’s greeting from the mountains
stations.text: In 1868 Brahms sent Clara Schumann a melody from the Bernese Alps, with the words: “High on the mountain, deep in the valley, I greet you many thousand times.” Eight years later a horn sings a version of that greeting in the finale of his First Symphony. The strings tremble beneath it; flutes take over the call. Then trombones and bassoons play a short chorale. The great string tune of the main Allegro is still to come, but Brahms has already planted his ending: this compact chorale will return, blazing, in the coda.

cues.text: The long wind call stretches above strings trembling on rapidly repeated notes.
Trombones and bassoons play a short chorale. Brahms saves its next appearance for the coda.
The call subsides, leaving room for the main Allegro that follows this excerpt.

stations.title: Bruckner keeps the strings running
stations.text: A little repeated figure in the strings starts the Seventh’s scherzo in A minor. Over it comes a trumpet call, answered by clarinet; that small exchange will help fill a movement of enormous orchestral surges. Bruckner keeps returning to the same scraps, moving them between instruments and building them into long crescendos. Between the outbursts, the brass can be unexpectedly gentle: trombones and tuba join a soft chorale while the strings keep moving. Another swell gathers before the excerpt ends. Beyond it lies the slower F-major trio, with a violin song introduced by quiet timpani.

cues.text: A small repeated string figure starts the scherzo; a trumpet call rises above it.
Brass and timpani join the rushing strings in the first great outburst.
Trombones and tuba play softly within the quieter passage; the strings remain busy beneath them.
The strings gather winds and brass into another crescendo before the slower trio.

stations.title: Tchaikovsky lets the basses fade
stations.text: In Klin on 23 February 1893, Tchaikovsky told his nephew Vladimir Davydov that the Sixth would end with “the most drawn-out Adagio”. He was delighted with the new symphony. Here, after the low-brass chorale, a melody previously heard in D major returns in B minor. It still has strength for one last swell. Then the orchestra falls away around the low strings, and the double basses keep repeating B as the sound thins. Their pulse grows softer until it can scarcely be heard.

cues.text: The second theme returns in B minor, over the low B in the basses.
The strings rise into one last swell before the long retreat.
The remaining phrase sinks towards the low strings and their repeated bass pulse.
The double basses’ B grows softer as the symphony reaches its quiet end.

stations.title: Mahler leaves room for silence
stations.text: The last page of Mahler’s Ninth begins with muted second violins. Adagissimo: slower still. Only strings remain, and the long melodies of the finale have broken into phrases of a few notes, separated by rests. Each attempt to continue seems to cost more time. The earlier climaxes are far behind, yet these tiny phrases keep finding somewhere to go. One note hangs after its companions have gone; another softly answers it. A viola’s small upward turn sounds inside the last D♭-major chord.

cues.text: Adagissimo: muted second violins begin the final page, with strings alone and long rests between phrases.
The viola turns its phrase upwards inside the last D♭-major chord; the remaining notes fade.
